docs.title: Inertial Navigation Simulation & GUI
docs.text:
ins_sim is an open-source 6-DOF, WGS-84 strapdown INS Monte Carlo simulator with a desktop GUI. It generates a truth flight trajectory, derives the gyro and accelerometer outputs a perfect IMU would produce along it, corrupts them with a navigation-grade IMU error model, and runs a strapdown mechanization to recover position, velocity, and attitude. A Monte Carlo ensemble over independent noise realizations characterizes how navigation error grows over time for a given IMU grade.

Download the app View on GitHub

docs.title: Core features
docs.text:
• Truth trajectory generation from YAML mission profiles — waypoint legs, speed ramps, climbs, and turns, specified in conventional aviation units and converted to strict SI internally.
  • Navigation-grade IMU error model: angular/velocity random walk, Gauss-Markov bias drift, turn-on bias repeatability, scale-factor and misalignment errors, and initial-alignment errors, parameterized by a YAML datasheet spec.
  • Rotating-Earth strapdown mechanization: Earth rate, transport rate, WGS-84 radii of curvature, and Somigliana normal gravity evaluated at the current latitude/altitude every step — not a flat-Earth approximation.
  • Vertical channel physics: a third-order baro-damped loop by default, or free-inertial mode to observe the channel's inherent instability.
  • Monte Carlo evaluation: ensembles of independent noise realizations with CEP, per-axis error bands, and percentile statistics.
  • Interactive visualizations — every tab is a plotly page rendered in-app: CEP growth with a percentile table, attitude/velocity/position 3σ bands, a 3D trajectory with a 95th percentile error tube, and a ground-track map.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Data flows from truth generation, through noise injection, into the strapdown navigator, and is summarized by the Monte Carlo / evaluation layer:

flowchart TD
    CFG["Config (YAML)<br/>trajectory + IMU spec"]
    TRUTH["Truth generation<br/>trajectory/kinematics.py"]
    SENSOR["Noise addition<br/>sensors/imu.py"]
    NAV["Strapdown mechanization<br/>navigation/strapdown.py"]
    EVAL["Monte Carlo + plots<br/>evaluation/"]
    EARTH(["Earth model<br/>core/earth_model.py"])

    CFG --> TRUTH
    TRUTH -->|"true ω, specific force"| SENSOR
    SENSOR -->|"measured ω, f (+ noise)"| NAV
    NAV -->|"pos, vel, attitude"| EVAL
    EARTH -.->|"ω_ie, ω_en, g, R_N/R_E"| TRUTH
    EARTH -.-> NAV

docs.title: Conventions in brief
docs.text:
• Frames: local-level North-East-Down navigation frame (n) and a vehicle-fixed body frame (b: x forward, y right, z down).
  • Attitude: scalar-last quaternion [x, y, z, w] representing the body-to-NED rotation, per the scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation convention.
  • Units: strict SI inside the simulation core; YAML configs use conventional datasheet/aviation units (deg, kt, ft, °/hr, µg) and are converted at load time.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Download & Install — grab the prebuilt app for Windows (x86-64) or Linux (x86-64 / ARM64, including Raspberry Pi 4/5 on 64-bit OS).
  • User Guide — configuring missions and reading the results.
  • Theory & Math — the formulations behind the simulator.

docs.title: Download & Install
docs.text:
Prebuilt portable bundles for Windows and Linux (x86-64 and ARM64) are attached to every GitHub Release. No Python installation is required — download, extract, and run.

Download for Windows Download for Linux

On the release page, grab the asset for your platform:

Platform Asset Run Windows (64-bit) ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-windows-x86_64.zip extract, run ins_sim.exe Linux (x86-64) ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-x86_64.tar.gz extract, run ins_sim Linux (ARM64) ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-aarch64.tar.gz extract, run ins_sim

Which Linux asset?

Run uname -m on the target machine: x86_64 → use the x86-64 asset; aarch64 → use the ARM64 asset. The ARM64 bundle covers Raspberry Pi 4/5 running the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS and other ARM64/aarch64 Linux. 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS (armv7l) is not covered by a prebuilt bundle — see Raspberry Pi (32-bit) below.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Download the .zip asset and extract it anywhere (no installer).
  2. Open the extracted ins_sim folder and run ins_sim.exe.

Windows SmartScreen

The binaries are not code-signed, so the first launch may show "Windows protected your PC". Click More info → Run anyway. Keep ins_sim.exe inside its folder — it needs the bundled libraries beside it.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Pick the asset matching your CPU (uname -m) — x86_64 or aarch64:

# Intel/AMD 64-bit
tar xzf ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
./ins_sim/ins_sim

# ARM64 (aarch64)
tar xzf ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-aarch64.tar.gz
./ins_sim/ins_sim

Runtime requirements

Bundles are built on Ubuntu 24.04, so a similarly recent glibc is required. Minimal installations may also need the Qt WebEngine system libraries:

sudo apt-get install libegl1 libgl1 libxkbcommon0 libnss3 libasound2t64

docs.title: Raspberry Pi
docs.text:
The ARM64 bundle (ins_sim-vX.Y.Z-linux-aarch64.tar.gz) is the one for a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 — but only when it is running the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS. Confirm first:

uname -m        # aarch64  → use the ARM64 bundle
                # armv7l   → 32-bit OS, see below

docs.title: Raspberry Pi (32-bit)
docs.text:
There is no prebuilt bundle for 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS (armv7l/armhf), and the desktop GUI cannot be installed there either — PySide6 publishes no 32-bit ARM wheels, so pip install ".[gui]" will not resolve. Two options, best first:

  1. Reflash to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS (the Pi 4/5 support it) and use the aarch64 bundle above, or run the GUI from source.

  2. Stay on 32-bit and run the headless CLI from source — it needs only numpy/scipy/pyyaml/matplotlib/plotly, no Qt:

    git clone https://github.com/jorgieo/ins_sim.git
cd ins_sim
pip install -e .          # base install, NOT ".[gui]"
python main.py            # writes an interactive maps/trajectory_map.html

    This produces the matplotlib summary figure and a standalone interactive ground-track map (open maps/trajectory_map.html in a browser) without the desktop front end. See the CLI options with python main.py --help.

docs.title: Internet access
docs.text: The application runs fully offline with one exception: the Map tab loads OpenStreetMap basemap tiles from the network. Every other visualization works without a connection.

docs.title: Run from source
docs.text:
Prefer a Python environment? Clone the repository and launch the GUI directly:

git clone https://github.com/jorgieo/ins_sim.git
cd ins_sim
pip install ".[gui]"
python -m ins_sim.gui

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: This guide walks through operating the desktop app, interpreting each visualization, and authoring your own mission and IMU configuration files.

docs.title: Running your first simulation
docs.text:
1. Select a trajectory. The Trajectory list shows the mission YAMLs in the trajectories folder next to the app: the app's own folder for the downloaded bundle, or the current working directory when run from source. On first launch the folder is created and seeded with the packaged bqn_departure.yaml. Files you add or edit there appear the next time you open the list, and your edits are never overwritten. Browse… opens the same folder and accepts any mission file with a top-level phases list. If that location is not writable, the app uses ~/ins_sim/trajectories instead.
  2. Select an IMU spec. Same pattern, with the imu_specs folder and the packaged navigation-grade imu_spec.yaml. Files must have top-level gyro and accel sections.
  3. Set the ensemble size. Monte Carlo iterations (default 50) trades statistical confidence against run time — ensemble statistics converge as \(1/\sqrt{N}\), so quadrupling the trials halves the noise on the percentile curves.
  4. Set the time step. Time step (dt) (default 0.1 s) is the truth and integration sample interval. 0.1 s is the reference setting; 0.5–1.0 s runs much faster and is fine for quick looks at long-duration error growth.
  5. Choose the vertical channel. Baro altitude aiding (checked by default) runs the third-order baro-damped vertical loop. Uncheck it to see the free-inertial vertical channel diverge — the instability is real physics, not a bug (see Theory & Math).
  6. Pick visualizations. Each checked box becomes one tab after the run.
  7. Run. The simulation executes on a background thread — the log pane streams progress (per-trial completion, timing, final 95th-percentile error) and the progress bar tracks the ensemble. The UI stays responsive throughout; controls re-enable when the run finishes.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
Every tab is an interactive plotly page — hover for values, drag to zoom, double-click to reset.

CEP (Circular Error Probable) — every trial's horizontal error in nautical miles against decimal hours, with the ensemble CEP drift-rate fit (fitted to the pointwise 50th percentile over the first hour). Below the plot, a table lists the 50th and 95th percentile error at each whole hour.

Attitude / Velocity / Position Errors — per-axis ensemble mean error with ±3σ bands, where σ is the sample standard deviation across trials. All three are resolved along the local North, East and Down axes at the true position, and every error is the estimate minus the truth (see Notation & conventions):

  • Attitude shows the small rotation between the estimated and the true attitude: the North and East tilts, and the heading error (the rotation about Down), in degrees.
  • Velocity and Position show the North, East and Down components. The position error is the latitude, longitude and height error converted to metres.

With baro aiding on, the Down channels stay bounded while North/East grow with the classic INS error signature; with aiding off, watch the Down channels run away.

3D Trajectory — the truth track (black), every trial's estimated track (steel blue), and the crimson swept tube of the 95th-percentile radial error.

Ground Track Map — the mission over OpenStreetMap tiles with the 95th-percentile horizontal-error envelope drawn perpendicular to the track and 5-minute markers along the truth path. The basemap tiles are the only part of the app that needs an internet connection.

docs.title: Writing mission profiles
docs.text:
A mission YAML has three top-level sections — departure, simulation_time, and phases. All angles are degrees, altitudes feet, speeds knots (or Mach); everything is converted to SI internally.

name: My Mission

departure:
  lat_deg:  18.4949        # start latitude
  lon_deg: -67.1294        # start longitude
  alt_ft:   237.0          # field elevation (MSL)
  nav_bank_angle_deg: 25.0 # bank angle used for inter-waypoint turns

simulation_time:
  dt_s: 0.1                # sample rate hint (GUI/CLI dt overrides it)

phases:
  - type: ground_roll
    ...

Phases execute in order; each starts from the state the previous one left (position, speed, heading, altitude).

Phase type Keys Behavior ground_roll heading_deg, run_length_m, speed_final_kt Accelerates along the runway heading over the given ground run. takeoff heading_deg, pitch_deg, speed_kt, duration_s Rotates and climbs out at the given pitch and speed. climb pitch_deg, speed_kt, to_altitude_ft Climbs at constant pitch/speed until reaching the target altitude. waypoint lat_deg, lon_deg, alt_ft, speed_kt (optional), loiter (optional) Flies a great-circle-style leg to the fix, turning at the departure-block bank angle. If speed_kt is omitted the leg inherits the current speed — e.g. a sprint leg flown at the Mach set by a preceding speed_ramp. speed_ramp speed_end_kt or speed_end_mach, duration_s Linear acceleration/deceleration to the target speed. speed_end_mach converts via the ISA sound speed at the current altitude.

The optional loiter block on a waypoint flies constant-bank circles on arrival:

loiter:
  n_turns:        5
  bank_angle_deg: 30.0
  direction:      right    # or left; default right

docs.title: Writing IMU specifications
docs.text:
An IMU YAML has gyro, accel, and optional alignment sections, all in conventional datasheet units; load_imu_spec converts to SI at load time.

name: Navigation-Grade RLG INS

gyro:
  arw_deg_per_rt_hr:        0.002   # Angular Random Walk [°/√hr]
  bias_instab_deg_per_hr:   0.01    # Bias instability (GM 1σ) [°/hr]
  bias_tau_s:               3600.0  # GM correlation time [s]
  repeatability_deg_per_hr: 0.01    # Turn-on bias repeatability 1σ [°/hr]
  scale_factor_ppm:         5.0     # Scale-factor error 1σ per axis [ppm]
  misalignment_urad:        50.0    # Axis misalignment 1σ per element [µrad]

accel:
  vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr:    0.005   # Velocity Random Walk [m/s/√hr]
  bias_instab_ug:           5.0     # Bias instability (GM 1σ) [µg]
  bias_tau_s:               3600.0  # GM correlation time [s]
  repeatability_ug:         25.0    # Turn-on bias repeatability 1σ [µg]
  scale_factor_ppm:         100.0   # Scale-factor error 1σ per axis [ppm]
  misalignment_urad:        50.0    # Axis misalignment 1σ per element [µrad]

alignment:
  tilt_std_deg:    0.0015   # initial N/E tilt error 1σ [°]
  heading_std_deg: 0.04     # initial azimuth error 1σ [°]
Key Physical meaning arw_deg_per_rt_hr / vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr White-noise density. Integrated angle (velocity) uncertainty grows as ARW·√t (VRW·√t). bias_instab_* + bias_tau_s In-run bias drift, modeled as a first-order Gauss-Markov process with the given steady-state 1σ and correlation time. repeatability_* Turn-on bias: a constant offset drawn once per trial. scale_factor_ppm Per-axis multiplicative error, drawn once per trial. misalignment_urad Sensor-triad axis misalignment, six independent small angles drawn once per trial. alignment: block Residual error of a stationary gyrocompass alignment, applied to the initial attitude of each trial. Physically, tilt ≈ accel repeatability / g and heading ≈ east-gyro repeatability / (Ωie cos φ) — the packaged 0.04° corresponds to 0.01 °/hr at ≈18.5° N.

scale_factor_ppm, misalignment_urad, and the alignment block are optional and default to zero (exact passthrough), so minimal diagnostic specs stay valid.

docs.title: Scripted workflows
docs.text:
The GUI and CLI drive the same engine. Headless run with the bundled defaults, or any custom files:

python main.py --config path/to/mission.yaml --imu-spec path/to/imu.yaml \
               --trials 100 --dt 0.1 --seed 7

Or call the pipeline directly from Python:

from ins_sim.trajectory.kinematics import build_trajectory
from ins_sim.sensors.imu import load_imu_spec
from ins_sim.evaluation.monte_carlo import run_monte_carlo, percentile_envelope

truth, v_sprint, R_turn = build_trajectory("mission.yaml", tau_i=0.1)
spec = load_imu_spec("imu_spec.yaml")

mc = run_monte_carlo(truth, spec, n_trials=100, seed=7, baro_aiding=True)
r95 = percentile_envelope(mc.est_r_lb_l, truth.r_lb_l, q=95)

Python names follow the symbols on the Notation & conventions page: for example, truth.r_lb_l is the true position relative to the start point, and mc.est_r_lb_l holds every trial's estimate of it.

The documentation figures on this site are produced by exactly this pipeline — see tools/generate_doc_plots.py in the repository.

docs.title: Bibliography
docs.text:
Works cited in these pages. Equation and section numbers quoted from Groves always refer to the second edition (2013); the first edition (2008) numbers its equations differently.

These docs follow Groves' notation. Every derivation, figure and table here is written fresh, and none is reproduced from the book.

docs.title: Inertial navigation
docs.text: Groves (2013) P. D. Groves, Principles of GNSS, Inertial, and Multisensor Integrated Navigation Systems, 2nd ed. Boston, MA: Artech House, 2013. The source of the notation used throughout these docs. Titterton & Weston (2004) D. H. Titterton and J. L. Weston, Strapdown Inertial Navigation Technology, 2nd ed. Stevenage, UK: IET, 2004. Savage (1998a) P. G. Savage, "Strapdown inertial navigation integration algorithm design, part 1: Attitude algorithms," Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 19–28, 1998. Savage (1998b) P. G. Savage, "Strapdown inertial navigation integration algorithm design, part 2: Velocity and position algorithms," Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, vol. 21, no. 2, pp. 208–221, 1998.

docs.title: Earth model
docs.text: NGA (2014) National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984: Its Definition and Relationships with Local Geodetic Systems, NGA.STND.0036_1.0.0_WGS84, 2014.

docs.title: Inertial sensor errors
docs.text: IEEE Std 952 IEEE Standard Specification Format Guide and Test Procedure for Single-Axis Interferometric Fiber Optic Gyros, IEEE Std 952-1997. Defines angle random walk and bias instability through the Allan variance. El-Sheimy et al. (2008) N. El-Sheimy, H. Hou, and X. Niu, "Analysis and modeling of inertial sensors using Allan variance," IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement, vol. 57, no. 1, pp. 140–149, 2008.

docs.title: Estimation
docs.text: Van Loan (1978) C. F. Van Loan, "Computing integrals involving the matrix exponential," IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, vol. 23, no. 3, pp. 395–404, 1978.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms and abbreviations used across these pages. Hover over any of them elsewhere in the docs to see the same definition as a tooltip. Symbols (such as \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) or \(R_N\)) are defined on the Notation & conventions page.

ARW Angle random walk: gyro white noise. Integrated angle uncertainty grows as ARW·√t; datasheets quote it in °/√h. CEP Circular error probable: the radius of the circle, centred on the true position, that contains 50% of horizontal position errors. ECEF Earth-centred, Earth-fixed frame (e): rotates with the Earth. ECI Earth-centred inertial frame (i): does not rotate with the Earth. GM First-order Gauss–Markov process: exponentially correlated random noise with a steady-state standard deviation and a correlation time. GNSS Global navigation satellite system (GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou). IMU Inertial measurement unit: three gyros and three accelerometers on orthogonal axes. INS Inertial navigation system: an IMU plus the navigation equations that turn its outputs into position, velocity and attitude. ISA International Standard Atmosphere: the reference profile of temperature and pressure with altitude. MEMS Micro-electro-mechanical systems: low-cost silicon inertial sensors. MSL Mean sea level. NED North-East-Down: the local navigation frame (n) used throughout ins_sim. QNH The altimeter pressure setting that makes a barometric altimeter read field elevation on the ground. RLG Ring laser gyroscope: an optical gyro technology used in navigation-grade INS. VRW Velocity random walk: accelerometer white noise. Integrated velocity uncertainty grows as VRW·√t; datasheets quote it in m/s/√h. WGS-84 World Geodetic System 1984: the reference ellipsoid, Earth rotation rate and gravity model used by ins_sim.

docs.title: Theory & Math
docs.text:
Notation transition

This page still uses the v0.2 symbols. In particular, \(R_N\) below is the transverse radius of curvature and \(\phi\) is latitude. The theory section is being rewritten in the notation of Groves (2013); see Notation & conventions for the symbols it will use.

This page documents the physics and mathematics as implemented in the simulator, with pointers to the modules that carry each formulation. Symbols: geodetic latitude \(\phi\), longitude \(\lambda\), altitude \(h\); NED navigation frame \(n\); body frame \(b\); body-to-NED rotation \(\mathbf{C}_b^n\).

docs.title: WGS-84 Earth model
docs.text:
Module: ins_sim/core/earth_model.py

Constant Symbol Value Semi-major axis \(a\) 6 378 137.0 m Flattening \(f\) 1 / 298.257223563 First eccentricity² \(e^2 = f(2-f)\) 6.694379990e−3 Earth rotation rate \(\omega_{ie}\) 7.2921151467e−5 rad/s

The radii of curvature at latitude \(\phi\):

\[ R_N = \frac{a}{\sqrt{1 - e^2\sin^2\phi}}, \qquad R_M = \frac{a\,(1 - e^2)}{\left(1 - e^2\sin^2\phi\right)^{3/2}} \]

where \(R_N\) (prime-vertical) governs east-west motion and \(R_M\) (meridian) governs north-south motion.

Earth rate and transport (craft) rate resolved in NED, both evaluated at the current state on every integration step:

\[ \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n = \begin{bmatrix} \omega_{ie}\cos\phi \\ 0 \\ -\omega_{ie}\sin\phi \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{v_E}{R_N + h} \\[2ex] \dfrac{-v_N}{R_M + h} \\[2ex] \dfrac{-v_E\tan\phi}{R_N + h} \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: Gravity
docs.text:
Normal gravity on the ellipsoid follows the Somigliana formula,

\[ g_0(\phi) = g_e\,\frac{1 + k\sin^2\phi}{\sqrt{1 - e^2\sin^2\phi}}, \qquad g_e = 9.7803253359~\text{m/s}^2,\quad k = 1.93185265241\times10^{-3}, \]

with a linear free-air altitude correction as implemented:

\[ g(\phi, h) = g_0(\phi)\left(1 - \frac{2h}{a}\right) \]

This first-order correction (\(\partial g/\partial h \approx -2g/a\)) omits the \(f\), \(m\) and \(h^2\) terms of the full WGS-84 formula. Against the full formula it overstates gravity by about 2 µg per kilometre of height at low latitudes: about 7 µg at the packaged mission's 15,000 ft cruise altitude (18.5° N) and up to 14 µg at 10 km, comparable to a navigation-grade accelerometer's bias. The truth generator and the navigator share this model, so the approximation does not affect the simulated navigation errors. The local gravity vector is \(\mathbf{g}^n = [0,\, 0,\, +g(\phi,h)]^T\) (Down positive).

docs.title: Strapdown mechanization
docs.text:
Module: ins_sim/navigation/strapdown.py (strapdown_navgrade)

The mechanization integrates the classic NED navigation equations. In continuous form:

\[ \dot{\mathbf{C}}_b^n = \mathbf{C}_b^n\,\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ib}^b - \boldsymbol{\Omega}_{in}^n\,\mathbf{C}_b^n, \qquad \boldsymbol{\Omega} = [\boldsymbol{\omega}\times] \] \[ \dot{\mathbf{v}}^n = \mathbf{C}_b^n\,\mathbf{f}^b - \left(2\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n\right) \times \mathbf{v}^n + \mathbf{g}^n \] \[ \dot{\phi} = \frac{v_N}{R_M + h}, \qquad \dot{\lambda} = \frac{v_E}{(R_N + h)\cos\phi}, \qquad \dot{h} = -v_D \]

Discretely, each step \(k \to k+1\) performs:

  1. Evaluate \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n\), \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n\), and \(g(\phi,h)\) at the current state.
  2. Form the body rate relative to the navigation frame: \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b = \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ib}^b - \mathbf{C}_n^b\left(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n\right)\).
  3. Attitude — advance by the exact rotation-vector exponential rather than a first-order DCM update: the implementation stores attitude as a scalar-last quaternion and right-multiplies by \(\exp\!\left([\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b\,\Delta t\,\times]\right)\), which is exactly the solution of the DCM differential equation above for a constant rate over the step.
  4. Resolve specific force into NED: \(\mathbf{f}^n = \mathbf{C}_b^n\mathbf{f}^b\).
  5. Velocity — forward-Euler step of the velocity equation, including the Coriolis term \(\left(2\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n\right)\times\mathbf{v}^n\).
  6. Position — forward-Euler step of the geodetic rates.

The forward-Euler scheme is chosen deliberately to match the truth-side IMU derivation: feeding the truth \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_{ib}^b, \mathbf{f}^b\) back through the mechanization reproduces the truth trajectory (the zero-noise self-consistency check in main.py).

docs.title: IMU stochastic error model
docs.text:
Module: ins_sim/sensors/imu.py (generate_imu_samples)

Each sensor triad's measurement is, per axis:

\[ \tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k = (\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{M})\,\mathbf{y}_k + \mathbf{b}_{r} + \mathbf{b}_{d,k} + \boldsymbol{\eta}_k \] Term Model Drawn \(\mathbf{M}\) Scale factor on the diagonal, six independent misalignment angles off-diagonal once per trial \(\mathbf{b}_r\) Turn-on bias repeatability, \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{BR}^2)\) once per trial \(\mathbf{b}_{d,k}\) Bias instability: first-order Gauss-Markov every sample \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_k\) ARW/VRW white noise every sample

The Gauss-Markov drift uses the exact discrete AR(1) form, which keeps the steady-state variance \(\sigma_{BI}^2\) independent of the sample rate. It starts from its stationary distribution, \(b_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{BI}^2)\), so its variance is \(\sigma_{BI}^2\) from the first sample:

\[ b_{k+1} = a\,b_k + \sqrt{1 - a^2}\,\sigma_{BI}\,w_k, \qquad a = e^{-\Delta t/\tau} \]

The white-noise standard deviation per sample is \(\sigma_\eta = \mathrm{ARW}/\sqrt{\Delta t}\) (VRW for the accelerometer), which makes the integrated angle (velocity) uncertainty grow as \(\mathrm{ARW}\cdot\sqrt{t}\) independent of the sample rate.

Each trial also draws an initial-alignment error: NED tilt and azimuth misalignments applied to the truth attitude, \(\mathbf{R}_0 = \exp([\boldsymbol{\delta}\times])\,\mathbf{R}_{0,\text{true}}\) with \(\boldsymbol{\delta} = [\delta_N, \delta_E, \delta_D]\). Physically the tilts are limited by accelerometer bias over \(g\) and the azimuth by the gyrocompass limit, east-gyro bias over \(\omega_{ie}\cos\phi\).

docs.title: Schuler oscillation
docs.text:
Horizontal position/velocity/tilt errors are coupled through gravity and the Earth's curvature into the Schuler loop: a tilt error \(\delta\theta\) misresolves gravity into horizontal acceleration \(g\,\delta\theta\), while the resulting position error re-tilts the computed local level by \(\delta p / R\). The result is a bounded oscillation with

\[ \omega_s = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R}}, \qquad T_s = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R}{g}} \approx 84.4~\text{min} \]

visible as the dominant period in the North/East error channels:

docs.title: Vertical channel
docs.text:
The vertical channel is unstable in a free-inertial mechanization. Perturbing the altitude equation through the free-air gravity gradient gives

\[ \delta\ddot{h} \approx \frac{2g}{R}\,\delta h + \delta a_D \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = \pm\sqrt{\frac{2g}{R}}, \]

an exponential divergence with e-folding time \(\sqrt{R/2g} \approx 570\) s (≈9.5 min). Uncheck Baro altitude aiding in the GUI to observe it.

With aiding enabled, the INS-minus-baro altitude residual drives a third-order damping loop acting on altitude, vertical velocity, and an integral state that absorbs steady vertical accelerometer error:

\[ K_1 = \frac{3}{\tau}, \qquad K_2 = \frac{3}{\tau^2}, \qquad K_3 = \frac{1}{\tau^3} \]

which places a triple pole at \(s = -1/\tau\) — characteristic polynomial \((s + 1/\tau)^3\) — with \(\tau = 100\) s by default: well-damped, no residual oscillation, and steady accelerometer bias rejected by the integrator.

docs.title: Monte Carlo error characterization
docs.text:
Module: ins_sim/evaluation/monte_carlo.py

The simulator characterizes navigation error empirically: \(N\) independent trials each draw their own turn-on biases, scale factor/misalignment matrices, Gauss-Markov histories, white-noise streams, and initial-alignment error, run the full nonlinear mechanization, and the ensemble is summarized statistically:

  • ±3σ bands (attitude/velocity/position tabs): the pointwise ensemble mean and standard deviation of each error component — the diagonal of the empirical covariance
\[ \mathbf{P}_{\text{emp}}(t) = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[\mathbf{x}_i(t) - \bar{\mathbf{x}}(t)\right] \left[\mathbf{x}_i(t) - \bar{\mathbf{x}}(t)\right]^T \]
  • Percentile envelopes: the pointwise \(q\)-th percentile of radial error across trials — the 95th percentile drives the 3D error tube and the map envelope.
  • CEP (Circular Error Probable): the pointwise 50th percentile of horizontal radial error, with a linear drift-rate fit over the first hour.

Ensemble statistics converge as \(1/\sqrt{N}\); the tails (95th percentile) converge more slowly than the median, so CEP stabilizes at lower trial counts than the error tube.

Not a linearized covariance analysis

The simulator propagates no linearized error-state model — there is no 15-state \(\dot{\delta\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{F}\delta\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{G}\mathbf{w}\) system or analytic covariance in the codebase. Every statistic above comes from full nonlinear Monte Carlo trials. Implementing the linearized model (and eventually Kalman-filter-based aiding, e.g. GNSS/INS) and validating it against these empirical bounds is natural future work.

docs.title: Notation & conventions
docs.text:
Inertial navigation keeps track of several reference frames at once: the spinning Earth, the local North-East-Down directions, and the vehicle's own axes. Most confusion in INS mathematics comes from losing track of which frame a quantity describes, relative to what, and along which axes its components are written. These docs use the notation of Groves (2013), which writes all three facts into every symbol.

This page is the reference for every symbol used elsewhere in the docs. Each symbol has one meaning on every page. From v0.3.0 the Python code uses the same scheme, so an equation and the line of code that implements it share their names.

Key points

  • A kinematic symbol reads "motion of the object frame, relative to the reference frame, resolved in the axes frame": \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) is the angular rate of the body (b) relative to inertial space (i), expressed along the body axes (b).
  • \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) transforms a vector's components from body axes to North-East-Down axes.
  • A tilde marks a sensor measurement and a hat marks an estimate. Errors are always estimate minus truth.
  • Everything inside the simulator is in SI units.

docs.title: Reading a Groves symbol
docs.text:
Every kinematic vector carries three frame labels:

\[ \huge \boldsymbol{\omega}_{\textcolor[RGB]{232,89,12}{i}\,\textcolor[RGB]{28,126,214}{b}}^{\textcolor[RGB]{47,158,68}{b}} \] Slot In \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) Meaning Main symbol \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) The quantity: here, angular rate. First subscript i The reference frame the motion is measured relative to. Here: inertial space. Second subscript b The object frame whose motion is described. Here: the vehicle body. Superscript b The resolving axes: the frame whose axes the three components are written along. Here: the body axes.

The resolving axes can change without changing the physical quantity. The same velocity vector, resolved in two different frames, is related by a transformation matrix:

\[ \vvec{eb}{n} = \Cmat{b}{n}\,\vvec{eb}{b} \]

Three symbols are worth reading aloud, because they are what the sensors measure and what the navigator outputs:

  • \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) is what a gyro triad measures: the body's rotation rate relative to inertial space, along the sensor axes.
  • \(\fvec{ib}{b}\) is what an accelerometer triad measures: specific force (acceleration relative to inertial space, minus gravitation), along the sensor axes.
  • \(\vvec{eb}{n}\) is the ground velocity the navigator reports: the body's velocity relative to the Earth, in North, East and Down components.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text: Frame Label Origin Axes Role in ins_sim Earth-centred inertial (ECI) i Earth's centre Fixed relative to the distant stars The frame gyros and accelerometers measure motion against. Earth-centred, Earth-fixed (ECEF) e Earth's centre Rotate with the Earth at \(\omega_{ie}\) Velocity is Earth-referenced. Local navigation (NED) n The vehicle North, East, Down at the current position Attitude and velocity are resolved here. Body b The IMU x forward, y right, z down The sensor axes. Local tangent plane l The start point North, East, Down at the start point Drawing tracks relative to the start.

docs.title: Transformation matrices
docs.text:
\(\Cmat{\beta}{\alpha}\) transforms a vector's components from the \(\beta\)-frame axes to the \(\alpha\)-frame axes. These matrices are orthonormal, so the inverse transformation is the transpose:

\[ \Cmat{n}{b} = \left(\Cmat{b}{n}\right)^{\mathsf T} \]

docs.title: Skew-symmetric matrices
docs.text:
The cross product \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}\) can be written as a matrix product, \(\skew{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{b}\), with

\[ \skew{\mathbf{a}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -a_3 & a_2 \\ a_3 & 0 & -a_1 \\ -a_2 & a_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The upper-case Greek symbol denotes the skew-symmetric form of an angular rate, e.g. \(\Wmat{ie}{n} = \skew{\wvec{ie}{n}}\).

docs.title: Decorations
docs.text: Notation Meaning Example Tilde Measured by a sensor \(\wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b}\), the gyro output Hat Estimated or computed by the navigator \(\Cmat[\hat]{b}{n}\), the computed attitude \(\delta\) Error, always estimate minus truth: \(\delta x = \hat{x} - x\) \(\delta\vvec{eb}{n}\) \((-)\), \((+)\) Value before / after an update step \(\Cmat{b}{n}(+)\) Subscript \(k\) Sample (epoch) index \(\mathbf{x}_k\) \(\tau_i\) IMU output and integration interval 0.1 s by default

docs.title: Attitude
docs.text:
The vehicle's attitude is the transformation \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) from body axes to NED axes. It can also be described by three Euler angles: roll \(\phi_{nb}\), pitch \(\theta_{nb}\) and heading (yaw) \(\psi_{nb}\). \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) is built by rotating through heading about the Down axis, then pitch about the new y axis, then roll about the new x axis: a z-y-x sequence.

Quaternion component order

Groves writes the attitude quaternion \(\qvec{b}{n}\) scalar-first, \((q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3)\), with \(q_0\) the scalar part. The code stores it scalar-last, [x, y, z, w], because that is the convention of scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation. The two describe the same rotation; only the storage order differs.

docs.title: Position, Earth shape and gravity
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(L_b\) Geodetic latitude of the body \(\lambda_b\) Longitude of the body \(h_b\) Geodetic height above the WGS-84 ellipsoid \(R_0\), \(e\), \(f\) Equatorial radius, eccentricity and flattening of the ellipsoid \(\omega_{ie}\) Earth rotation rate (a scalar). Its vector form in NED is \(\wvec{ie}{n}\). \(R_N\) Meridian radius of curvature: governs north-south motion \(R_E\) Transverse radius of curvature: governs east-west motion \(\gvec{b}{n}\) Acceleration due to gravity at the body, resolved in NED (Down-positive) \[ R_N = \frac{R_0\,(1-e^2)}{\left(1-e^2\sin^2 L_b\right)^{3/2}}, \qquad R_E = \frac{R_0}{\sqrt{1-e^2\sin^2 L_b}} \]

Same letters, different meaning

Many geodesy and navigation texts write the meridian radius as \(M\) or \(R_M\), and the prime-vertical (normal) radius as \(N\) or \(R_N\). In those texts, \(R_N\) is Groves' \(R_E\). ins_sim v0.2 and earlier followed that convention. From v0.3.0 the code and these docs use Groves' \(R_N\) (meridian) and \(R_E\) (transverse).

Height

\(h_b\) is height above the ellipsoid. The simulator has no geoid model, so mission altitudes given above mean sea level (for example the YAML alt_ft key) are used directly as ellipsoidal height.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors are always the estimate minus the truth.

  • Attitude error \(\delta\psivec{nb}{n}\) is the small rotation that takes the true attitude to the computed one: \(\Cmat[\hat]{b}{n} \approx \left(\Ithree + \skew{\delta\psivec{nb}{n}}\right)\Cmat{b}{n}\). Its components are the North tilt, the East tilt and the Down (heading) error.
  • Velocity error \(\delta\vvec{eb}{n} = \vvec[\hat]{eb}{n} - \vvec{eb}{n}\).
  • Position error \(\delta\rvec{eb}{n}\), resolved in NED at the true position:
\[ \delta\rvec{eb}{n} = \begin{bmatrix} \left(R_N + h_b\right)\delta L_b \\ \left(R_E + h_b\right)\cos L_b\,\delta\lambda_b \\ -\delta h_b \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: IMU errors
docs.text:
The sensors' outputs are modelled as

\[ \fvec[\tilde]{ib}{b} = \mathbf{b}_a + \left(\Ithree + \mathbf{M}_a\right)\fvec{ib}{b} + \mathbf{w}_a, \qquad \wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b} = \mathbf{b}_g + \left(\Ithree + \mathbf{M}_g\right)\wvec{ib}{b} + \mathbf{w}_g \]

where each bias is split into a static and a dynamic part, \(\mathbf{b}_a = \mathbf{b}_{as} + \mathbf{b}_{ad}\) and \(\mathbf{b}_g = \mathbf{b}_{gs} + \mathbf{b}_{gd}\).

Term Meaning Drawn IMUSpec field YAML key \(\mathbf{b}_{gs}\), \(\mathbf{b}_{as}\) Static (turn-on) bias Once per trial gyro_br_std, accel_br_std repeatability_* \(\mathbf{b}_{gd}\), \(\mathbf{b}_{ad}\) Dynamic (in-run) bias: first-order Gauss–Markov Every sample *_bi_std, *_bi_tau bias_instab_*, bias_tau_s \(\mathbf{M}_g\), \(\mathbf{M}_a\) Scale factor (diagonal) and misalignment (off-diagonal) Once per trial *_sf_std, *_ma_std scale_factor_ppm, misalignment_urad \(\mathbf{w}_g\), \(\mathbf{w}_a\) White noise: ARW and VRW Every sample gyro_arw, accel_vrw arw_deg_per_rt_hr, vrw_m_per_s_per_rt_hr \(\delta\psivec{nb}{n}(0)\) Initial alignment error Once per trial align_tilt_std, align_heading_std alignment: block

Groves' gyro model also includes a g-dependent bias, proportional to specific force. ins_sim does not model it.

docs.title: Symbols and code names
docs.text:
The Python column lists the identifiers used from v0.3.0. They follow one pattern:

  • Vectors are <quantity>_<reference><object>_<axes>: \(\vvec{eb}{n}\) is v_eb_n.
  • Transformations are C_<from>_<to>: \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) is C_b_n.
  • Prefixes true_, meas_ and est_ mark truth, measurement and estimate where the role would otherwise be ambiguous.
Symbol Meaning SI unit Python (v0.3.0) v0.2 name Explained in \(L_b\), \(\lambda_b\), \(h_b\) Latitude, longitude, height rad, rad, m L_b, lambda_b, h_b lat, lon, alt Earth & gravity \(R_N\) Meridian radius of curvature m R_N R_M ⚠ Earth & gravity \(R_E\) Transverse radius of curvature m R_E R_N ⚠ Earth & gravity \(\wvec{ie}{n}\) Earth rate, NED rad/s omega_ie_n w_ie Earth & gravity \(\wvec{en}{n}\) Transport rate, NED rad/s omega_en_n w_en Earth & gravity \(\gvec{b}{n}\) Gravity, NED m/s² g_b_n g_n Earth & gravity \(\Cmat{b}{n}\) Attitude (scipy Rotation) – C_b_n R_b2n Frames & attitude \(\qvec{b}{n}\) Attitude quaternion, scalar-last – q_b_n quat Frames & attitude \(\phi_{nb}\), \(\theta_{nb}\), \(\psi_{nb}\) Roll, pitch, heading rad euler_nb euler Frames & attitude \(\wvec{ib}{b}\) True angular rate rad/s omega_ib_b omega_b Truth & ideal IMU \(\fvec{ib}{b}\) True specific force m/s² f_ib_b f_b Truth & ideal IMU \(\wvec[\tilde]{ib}{b}\) Gyro output rad/s meas_omega_ib_b omega_meas IMU errors \(\fvec[\tilde]{ib}{b}\) Accelerometer output m/s² meas_f_ib_b f_meas IMU errors \(\wvec{in}{n}\) Rate of n relative to i rad/s omega_in_n w_in Mechanization \(\wvec{nb}{b}\) Rate of b relative to n rad/s omega_nb_b w_nb_b Mechanization \(\vvec{eb}{n}\) Velocity, NED m/s v_eb_n vel_n, v_n Mechanization \(\rvec{lb}{l}\) Position relative to the start point m r_lb_l pos_n Mechanization \(\tau_i\) IMU and integration interval s tau_i dt Mechanization \(\avec{ib}{b}\), \(\uvec{ib}{b}\) Attitude and velocity increments rad, m/s alpha_ib_b, upsilon_ib_b – Mechanization \(\delta\psivec{nb}{n}\) Attitude error rad delta_psi_nb_n mis_rotvec (initial only) INS error model \(\delta\vvec{eb}{n}\) Velocity error m/s delta_v_eb_n – INS error model \(\delta\rvec{eb}{n}\) Position error, local NED m delta_r_eb_n – INS error model

User-facing names do not change: YAML keys, command-line flags and GUI labels keep their datasheet-style names. For example, the GUI's Time step (dt) is \(\tau_i\).

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Everything inside the simulator is SI: radians, metres, seconds, and quantities derived from them. Mission and IMU YAML files use the units of aviation charts and sensor datasheets (degrees, feet, knots, °/h, µg), and are converted to SI as they are loaded. The GUI converts back to familiar display units (degrees, nautical miles) only when plotting.
